title: Voice: self-triggered kill switch, crashes, liveness, screen lock
owns: app/voice/**, app/main/voice.ts, the announcement sentence in app/main/agent/host.ts (one small hunk), screen-lock handling (small hunks in main.ts / environment)

findings.title: Ember's own spoken announcement says “Say 'Ember, stop' to cancel.” and its microphone hearing it fires the kill switch (Windows, macOS, Linux without parec)
findings.platforms: windows, macos (and linux when parec/pulseaudio-utils is missing)
findings.scenario: A user on a Windows or macOS laptop, with “Speak replies” on (or Narrator/VoiceOver running, which also turns speaking on), says “Hey Ember, delete the build folder”. That is a D4.4 announced command: the bubble shows “It starts in 4 seconds”, and Ember speaks the announcement plus “Say 'Ember, stop' to cancel.” through the laptop speakers. The microphone hears Ember's own voice say “Ember, stop”. Windows and macOS have no speaker-output stream (speakerMonitor:false), so nothing rejects it, and the kill phrase deliberately works while Ember speaks. The engine emits stop, and main runs stopEverything('voice'). That cancels the command, or interrupts it half-run if the 4 s countdown has already elapsed (the phrase comes at the end of a 4-6 s sentence). It also aborts every other running task and command on every target. Headphones hide the problem; speakers do not.
findings.evidence: host.ts:1226 appends `Say 'Ember, stop' to cancel.` to every announcement, and main.ts:1545 speaks it via voice.speak(spokenText(text)). platform/win32/system/index.ts:77 and platform/darwin/system/index.ts:111 set speakerMonitor:false. engine.ts:583 and 748 let ember_stop through while Ember speaks, rejecting only when the speaker stream said it. I ran the real models (scratch script self-stop.cjs): with selfSpeaking(true), a TTS 'Ember, stop' on the mic and no speaker stream gives `stop` at gain 0.1, 0.3 and 1.0 (about -20 dB is enough); with the speaker stream present it gives `rejected:speakers`. In the real app (dev build, fake mic playing the clip while the voice process was told Ember is speaking), the log shows `voice.event stop` and `killswitch.pulled {source:'voice'}`. docs/COMMANDS-WSL-SSH.md:161 documents the spoken sentence but says nothing about this side effect, and it is not among L1-L26.
findings.fix: Never speak the kill phrase where Ember cannot tell its own voice from the user's. In host.ts, use the platform's stop chord words instead of the phrase (sc.stop.say, e.g. “Press Windows key, Alt, X to cancel”), or only append the phrase when speaker rejection is actually running (voice 'monitor' on). More generally, in the engine, while Ember speaks and no speaker stream is arriving (!hearsSpeakers), require ember_stop to stand well above Ember's own level, or accept only the chord. Also strip the wake and stop phrases from spokenText for platforms without a monitor.

findings.title: VoiceEngine.bargeIn transcribes an empty pre-roll ring; sherpa throws a bare WASM number out of feed() and the voice process dies
findings.platforms: linux (needs the parec speaker stream, so Linux with parec only)
findings.scenario: A wake window is open (the user said “Hey Ember” and Ember waits for the request; replayPreRoll has emptied the ring, and listening mode does not refill it). Ember then starts to speak, for example a finished task is announced. The user says “Hey Ember” again over it, and the speaker stream is live but did not say it. bargeIn() calls backend.transcribe(ring.read()) on 0 samples. sherpa's Moonshine throws a bare number; nothing catches it, so the exception escapes engine.feed() in process.ts's port handler. The utility process exits with code 1, and main shows “The voice process stopped. Trying again in 1 s…”. The user is deaf for the 3-6 s model reload and loses the request in progress; repeats climb the 1/5/30 s backoff.
findings.evidence: Deterministic repro with the real models (scratch repro-bargein.cjs): wake clip, wait for the check, selfSpeaking(true), feed the wake clip with the monitor stream live: 'EXCEPTION out of engine.feed(): number 92691224'. Stack: bargeIn engine.ts:769, decideStop:726, feed:599. A 15-minute randomized soak with real models threw the same number within about 60 s on 3 of 3 seeds, always from transcribe() on a zero-length array. A direct fuzz shows backend.transcribe throws a number for fewer than about 1000 samples (800 samples throws, 1600 does not). In an Electron utilityProcess, a throw in a MessagePort handler exits the process with code 1 (verified). Nothing else threw in four 20-minute soaks once short transcribes were guarded.
findings.fix: In sherpa.ts transcribe(): return '' (or zero-pad to 0.1 s) when samples.length < 1600, and wrap the recognizer calls in try/catch so a WASM exception can never kill the process. Also try/catch around engine.feed()/feedMonitor() in process.ts and report a 'voice.engine_error' instead of dying. In bargeIn(), skip the transcript when the ring is shorter than about 0.1 s.

findings.title: A damaged speech-model folder fails forever with the message “37825408”, and the only remedy (the download button) is hidden
findings.scenario: An antivirus quarantines or truncates a model file, a disk error or manual cleanup removes one, or a package is damaged, while the `.ok` marker stays. Turning on “Hey Ember” then shows “Not working: 37825408” (a WASM exception pointer). There is no retry and no explanation. Settings hides the “Download speech models” button because modelsReady() only checks the marker and the folder name, so the user cannot repair it without deleting the models folder by hand.
findings.evidence: Reproduced in the real app: truncate encode.int8.onnx in userData/models/sherpa-onnx-moonshine-tiny-en-int8 to 1000 bytes. Log: `voice.error {message:'37819256'}`; state 'error'; voice.modelsReady === true. Plain Node reproduces it too: sherpaBackend throws the number 37825408. process.ts:57 uses `err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)`, and sherpa-onnx's WASM exports no exception-message helper. models.ts:70 verified() trusts the marker; home/main.ts:800 hides the button when modelsReady. The unit test 'a model that won't load is an error to show' assumes a readable message.
findings.fix: Treat any failure to load the models as 'damaged': in the voice process turn non-Error throws into 'The speech models couldn't be loaded', and in VoiceService delete the .ok markers and go to needs-models with “The speech models look damaged. Download them again.” so the existing download button repairs it. Optionally verify file sizes at start.

findings.title: A dead-silent microphone is shown as “Listening for ‘Hey Ember’”
findings.scenario: The default input is a monitor or the wrong device, the laptop mic-mute key or GNOME's input mute is on, or an HDMI/unused input is selected. getUserMedia succeeds and frames arrive, all zeros. Ember reports 'Listening for “Hey Ember”' (settings line and handle icon) while it cannot hear anything, and nothing ever tells the user why “Hey Ember” does nothing. With no microphone at all, Ember also keeps the speech models loaded (297 MB working set measured) while only showing an error.
findings.evidence: Run with a 60 s all-silence fake mic: state stays 'waiting'; the only trace is the once-a-minute log line `voice.cpu {peak:0}`. process.ts accumulates `peak` and main/voice.ts:239 only logs it, and the watchdog only tests that frames arrive. With no device: state 'error', voice process 297 MB (getAppMetrics workingSetSize).
findings.fix: Use the peak that is already measured: if peak is exactly 0 (a live mic always has some noise floor) across about 30-60 s of frames, send a 'silent' message and have main show “The microphone is sending silence. Check the input device or mute switch in Sound settings.” (state error or a warning detail). Optionally start the voice process only once the mic page reports 'capturing'.

findings.title: teardown() right after utilityProcess.fork() kills nothing: the voice process is orphaned (about 300 MB) until Ember quits
findings.platforms: all (windows/macOS most exposed: slower process spawn)
findings.scenario: VoiceService.teardown() sets this.proc = null and calls p.kill(). Electron's UtilityProcess.kill() does nothing before the process has spawned, and main has dropped its handle, so a 'Ember voice' process with the models loaded stays alive for the rest of the session; each repeat adds another. Triggers are a mute or unmute double-press, or listening toggled off and on, within the spawn latency; or the mic page reporting a permission error within about 100 ms of start (macOS or Windows privacy denied) when spawning is slower than here.
findings.evidence: In the dev app, 4 start-then-teardown pairs each at gaps of 0, 5, 20, 50, 100 and 200 ms (a repeat run gave a different count): leaked processes at the 0 ms gap and once at 5 ms, none at 20 ms or more. In another run 3 survived 15 s later and after a forced GC; a same-tick storm left 22 voice processes alive (a synthetic worst case). On this Linux box fork-to-spawn is 9-37 ms against 70-150 ms for a permission-denied error, so it does not leak here; spawn is slower on Windows. I could not test Windows or macOS.
findings.fix: Keep the handle until exit: in teardown() call p.kill() and, if p.pid is undefined, also `p.once('spawn', () => p.kill())` (or track pending procs and kill on 'spawn'). Alternatively ask the child to exit by message.

findings.title: No liveness check on the voice process: if it hangs, the UI says “Listening” and the mic page queues audio without limit
findings.scenario: The frame watchdog runs inside the voice process, so a frozen or starved process (stuck WASM call, EDR/antivirus suspending it, thrashing) cannot report itself. Main only learns of a crash through 'exit'. Ember keeps showing “Listening for ‘Hey Ember’”, wake words do nothing, and the mic page keeps posting 64 KB/s into the MessagePort queue (about 230 MB per hour).
findings.evidence: SIGSTOP on the voice utility process for 25 s: voice state stayed 'waiting' with no restart or message; on SIGCONT it processed the backlog in a burst. No real hang trigger was found; the recognizers are bounded (21 s of audio takes 1.4 s).
findings.fix: Have the voice process send a heartbeat (it already ticks every second) and let VoiceService restart it when none arrives for about 10 s. A bounded queue or backpressure from the mic page would also cap memory.

findings.title: Spoken text drops asterisks that are not emphasis: “5 * 3 * 2” is read as “5 3 2” and “*.tmp” as “.tmp”
findings.scenario: Ember reads answers aloud (Speak replies, or a screen reader running). The italics rule treats `* ... *` pairs with spaces inside as emphasis, so multiplication and wildcard patterns lose their stars in what is said, while the bubble shows them. “Delete *.tmp and *.log” is spoken as “Delete .tmp and .log”, which also misreads a destructive command; `__init__` is said as “init”.
findings.evidence: Run: spokenText('Delete *.tmp and *.log from the folder.') → 'Delete .tmp and .log from the folder.'; 'That is 6 * 7 * 1 = 42.' → 'That is 6  7  1 = 42.'; 'Use __init__.py and a * b * c.' → 'Use init.py and a  b  c.' The regex is /(^|[\s(])[*_]([^*_\n]+)[*_](?=[\s.,!?;:)]|$)/.
findings.fix: Follow CommonMark flanking: the opening marker must be followed by a non-space and the closing one preceded by a non-space, e.g. /(^|[\s(])([*_])(?=\S)([^*_\n]*\S)\2(?=[\s.,!?;:)]|$)/, and do not treat `_` inside words or `__x__` in file names as emphasis.

findings.title: The model download sits at “100%” while the archives are verified and unpacked
findings.scenario: Progress counts compressed download bytes, so settings shows “Downloading speech models… 100%” while sha256 and in-process bzip2 unpacking run (the 107 MB Moonshine archive). That is long enough to look hung, and longer on 2-core machines or with antivirus scanning each written file.
findings.evidence: In the dev app the progress callback reached 100% at 3.4 s of an 8.6 s download-and-install (about 5 s at 100%, on 4 fast cores). The unpack alone took 8.9 s in the standalone test.
findings.fix: Report progress as (downloaded + unpacked) or cap the bar at about 90% until the move into place, and set the status text to “Unpacking…” once the last byte arrives.

findings.title: Speaker rejection's parec is pinned to the sink that was default at start and may keep the sink awake
findings.scenario: parec is started with --device=@DEFAULT_MONITOR@ once, when listening starts. PulseAudio resolves that name when the stream is created and does not move such a stream when the default sink changes. After the user plugs in headphones or a Bluetooth speaker, the monitor stays on the old sink: a video's “Hey Ember” or Ember's own voice through the new sink is no longer rejected, and Ember's barge-in logic believes the stream is alive (it still delivers silence). A permanent record stream on a monitor source also counts as activity, so the output device never idle-suspends (battery, DAC hiss).
findings.evidence: Not verified here: the container has no PulseAudio or parec. Based on PulseAudio's behaviour for streams created with an explicit source name, and on the code: speakers.ts starts parec once and only restarts it when it exits. No docs mention output-device changes.
findings.fix: Restart the monitor when the default sink changes (for example `pactl subscribe`, or the mic page's devicechange, which also fires for output devices), and mention the always-on monitor in the consent text or let it run only while Ember speaks or a wake is pending. Verify on RHEL 8 hardware with `pactl list short source-outputs` after switching sinks.

findings.title: Ember speaks aloud whenever a screen reader runs, with no way to turn it off, and the macOS module comment says the opposite
findings.scenario: maySpeak() is true whenever 'Speak replies' is on or a screen reader is detected. The user's 'Speak replies' switch cannot switch it off while a screen reader is running. Ember's own local voice then speaks answers, questions, task results and announcements at the same time as the screen reader reads the bubble's live region (or on top of it), so a user with a braille display or who prefers the reader's voice cannot get one voice. Only Ctrl+Alt+X (hush) stops it for the moment. darwin/system/a11y.ts's header says VoiceOver detection exists so 'Ember then doesn't speak over it', which is the reverse of what main.ts does; the Windows and Linux probes make the same call.
findings.evidence: main.ts:702 `policy.features.speak !== false && (settings.get().speak || sys.a11y.screenReaderOn())`; used at main.ts:689, 1513, 1529, 1545. Settings copy in home/index.html ('With a screen reader running, Ember also speaks its questions and results'). darwin/system/a11y.ts:2-3 header comment. Chromium cannot show how the reader and Ember overlap; this is from the code.
findings.fix: Make speech a three-way setting (Automatic when a screen reader runs / Always / Never) so an explicit 'Never' wins, and correct the macOS comment or decide the intended behaviour. If the reader reliably voices the live regions, speak only what they cannot (announcements, command questions).

findings.title: While the local screen is locked, Ember keeps listening for "Hey Ember" and keeps reading and speaking about the user's apps; only the borrowed mouse checks for a lock, and the Linux check can't see GNOME's lock shield
findings.scenario: The user locks the workstation (Super+L, idle lock) with Ember running and 'Hey Ember' on. The wake word is not speaker-specific, so anyone in the room says 'Hey Ember, what's in my open email?'. onVoice('utterance') goes straight to askEmber() with no lock check, accessibility keeps working for apps behind the shield, and the answer is spoken aloud (if speaking is on). Read-only tools need no confirmation, and apps granted 'Always' can be acted on. The docs say tasks stop when a REMOTE computer's screen locks (COMMANDS-WSL-SSH.md:418); the local PC has no such rule.
findings.evidence: Code path read end to end: voice.setWanted() depends only on settings (main.ts:1603); case 'utterance' (main.ts:891-903) calls askEmber(); no code under app/main/agent, perception or voice consults a lock state. XInput.screenLocked is used only by hands/borrow.ts:349. Its Linux implementation (hands/input.ts:477-488) looks only at XScreenSaver state ScreenSaverOn and DPMS-not-On, which GNOME Shell's lock shield does not set before the display blanks (stated from knowledge of GNOME; not reproduced, since there is no GNOME lock screen under Xvfb). macOS has CGSSessionScreenIsLocked, but only borrow uses it. Electron's powerMonitor 'lock-screen'/'unlock-screen' events (Windows, macOS) are not used; only 'resume' and 'shutdown' are.
findings.fix: Treat a locked or inactive local session like the remote case: stop listening (voice.teardown / mute) and refuse asks, speech and tasks while locked, and say so on return. Detect it with powerMonitor lock-screen/unlock-screen on Windows and macOS, and on Linux with logind LockedHint/Active (loginctl or org.gnome.ScreenSaver.GetActive over D-Bus), not only the X screensaver.
